children.author: battery_staple_
children.text:
My hobby project gets much less of my time than I would prefer. I've got the strongest model I have access to, on a cheap subscription, running --yolo in a VM with a fairly locked down firewall. I found that a tree (i.e. the filesystem) isn't really enough, for representing my thoughts, so I've built a graph datastore of sorts with a query layer that basically consists of a view (fitting the graph onto a tree) and a filter (for the root of that tree). Technically I've got a review process for the graph, but in practice I just approve it. I'm planning to build out an automated review process, kinda like unit tests, where I give a given prompt ownership over a specific cluster of nodes (and the code paths owned by them), and that prompt has to approve changes before I see them, but I haven't done that yet.

To answer your question, the actual review I do, is when the agent asks me questions. I tell it to resume a task, it asks questions, I answer them. If those questions are off-the-rails, I stop, pop the conceptual stack, and come at the whole thing from a different angle.

I'm basically trusting the model to do a good job, and fixing forward, always annealing the project toward what I want. And the rejection criteria is when the questions that it's asking are _questions I don't care about_.

source.text:
Just as title says, in the world of ai accelerated code production, when you're in charge of a repo or project, how do you usually look at code from proposed changes ?

I'm interested to find what your workflows look like these days.
source.title: Ask HN: In the new AI world, what's the best way to review code?
